notes:
I couldn't find any verse where Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican teachers really disagree. The commentators I read agree on what each verse means and differ only in emphasis. I also found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic or Orthodox sites, or prosperity or word-of-faith teaching, so those parts are left out. Notes from Ellicott (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-5.html, abbreviated "Ellicott page" below) are my own summaries with the URL given; I couldn't cite them line by line.

**v. 1**
- Matthew Henry: Reuben forfeited his birthright by defiling his father's concubine, and was, for that, sentenced not to excel, Gen. 49:4. The tribe was degraded, it was not discarded or disinherited. The birthright skipped Simeon, the next son, for it was typical, and therefore must attend, not the course of nature, but the choice of grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Guzik (Enduring Word, Calvary Chapel): the verse explains why Reuben, the firstborn, isn't listed first. It was because of the sin described in this verse, which disqualified Reuben from being first among the sons of Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): the birthright meant not only dominion, but a double portion (De 21:17), and both passed to Joseph, whose two adopted sons each became a tribe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-1.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: Reuben is still called "firstborn" because he was born first, even though the privileges went to Joseph's sons. Those sons were not, however, entered in the family register of the house of Israel according to the birthright. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-1.htm
- Gill: the list follows neither Reuben's natural birthright nor Joseph's birthright by gift; the reason comes in verse 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/5-1.html
- Ellicott (Anglican): the aside in verses 1–2 defends the legitimacy of David's line, since Reuben and Joseph both had earlier claims than Judah. He thinks the reading "to Joseph" found in some manuscripts may be the original. — Ellicott page

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: "the chief ruler" means David. He adds the New Testament point that our Lord came from Judah, and says the birthright was Joseph's, who actually received the "double portion" in the two tribal domains of Ephraim and Manasseh. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-2.htm
- Benson (Methodist): "Judah" means the tribe, not the man. Government was to rest in Judah, first in David and then in the Messiah, which was a far greater privilege than the birthright. Same URL.
- Matthew Henry: the two parts of the birthright were split. Judah got rule, and with it he needed not envy Joseph the double portion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Gill notes that the Syriac and Arabic versions read the "ruler" as the King Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: the same four clans appear in Genesis 46, Exodus 6 and Numbers 26. He finds it striking that Hezron and Carmi are also Judahite clan names. — Ellicott page

**vv. 4–6**
- Ellicott: the text implies but doesn't state how Joel connects to the four sons. The line runs seven generations to Beerah, who was deported around 734 BC. If no generations are skipped, Joel lived in the time of David and Solomon. The Greek translation (LXX) reads verse 4 differently. — Ellicott page
- v. 5, Ellicott: compares the name "Baal" with Saul's descendants Eshbaal and Meribbaal. — Ellicott page
- v. 6, JFB: there seem to have been carryings away of the people of Israel, the first by Pul (1 Chronicles 5:26), the second by Tiglath-pileser (1 Chronicles 5:6; 1 Chronicles 5:26), and the third by Shalmaneser. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-chronicles-5.html
- v. 6, Matthew Henry suggests Beerah may be named because he did not do his part to prevent the captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/5-17.html

**vv. 7–8**
- Ellicott: the four chiefs (Beerah, Jeiel, Zechariah, Bela) probably match Reuben's four clans. Bela's shorter family line doesn't mean he lived at a different time, because genealogies often skip names. He places Aroer, Nebo and Baal-meon east of the Dead Sea and notes all three appear on the Moabite Stone of King Mesha. — Ellicott page

**v. 9**
- JFB: if the land didn't reach the Euphrates under Moses or Joshua, it did under David, and grazing that far east affords an unmistakeable proof of the increase of their herds and flocks. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-chronicles-5.html
- Ellicott: "Gilead" here means all Israelite land east of the Jordan. The wording may show the account was first written in Babylonia. — Ellicott page

**v. 10**
- Clarke (via Guzik): the Hagrites were tribes of Nomade, or Scenite, Arabs; people who lived in tents, without any fixed dwellings, and whose property consisted in cattle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/
- JFB: the Septuagint has "the neighbours" instead of "the Hagarites." Individual tribes often waged separate wars even in Saul's reign. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-chronicles-5.html
- Ellicott: the Hagrites are sons of Hagar, an Arab people also named in Assyrian inscriptions. — Ellicott page

**vv. 11–12**
- JFB: Gad is listed with Reuben as these three were associated in a separate colony. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Ellicott: Salecah is modern Sulkhad. Since "in Bashan" is attached to them, the names probably stand for clans rather than single people. — Ellicott page

**vv. 13–15**
- Matthew Henry: Abihail's line is traced upward, from son to father, while verses 4–5 trace downward. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Ellicott: nothing more is known of Buz. Ahi may have been chief when the register was made. — Ellicott page

**v. 16**
- JFB: "Sharon" was used as descriptive of any place of extraordinary beauty and productiveness. This one lay east of the Jordan. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Ellicott disagrees: he thinks the old suggestion to read "Shirion" (Hermon) is probably right, since the well-known Sharon lies west of the Jordan. — Ellicott page

**v. 17**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the two kings didn't reign at the same time, so two different registrations must be referred to, and that carried on under Jotham is mentioned first, because Judah had the legitimate kingship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-17.htm
- Poole suggests it might instead be Jeroboam I, when the northern kingdom was new and needed to know its strength. JFB and Barnes say Jeroboam II. Same URL.
- Cambridge Bible: "reckoning by genealogy" is a phrase found only in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah. Its aim was not so much to take a census of them, as to inquire into the purity of their Israelite descent. Same URL.
- Matthew Henry: these lists were made just before the captivity, perhaps as a hint that though they were, for the present, cast out, they were not cast off for ever. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm

**v. 18**
- Matthew Henry: How much more considerable might Israel have been than they were in the time of the judges if all the tribes had acted in conjunction! https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Ellicott: the total is close to the 40,000 in Joshua 4:13 and probably comes from an official census. — Ellicott page

**v. 19**
- JFB: Jetur's descendants were the Itureans. Jerome traces Nodab to Kedemah, Ishmael's twelfth son. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-chronicles-5.html
- Ellicott: "Nodab" may be a copying error for Kedemah. — Ellicott page

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry: Though they had a powerful army, they relied not on that, but on the divine power. Also, it is the believing prayer that will be the prevailing prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Guzik: Because they put their trust in Him, God delivered them in the battle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/
- Gill: the help came from the Lord, perhaps after the battle at first went against them, and they trusted in his power and providence, and not in their own strength, courage, and military skill. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-20.htm
- Clarke: the Targum, an Aramaic paraphrase, says they trusted "in his Word." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/5-20.html
- Keil & Delitzsch: the wording shows the war was serious and the land itself was at stake. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-20.htm
- Biblical Illustrator, sounding a note of caution: It is not, however, every just cause that triumphs, and defeat is sometimes the lot of the innocent. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_chronicles/5-20.htm
- Modern-leaning note from Ellicott: the Arab warriors no doubt cried to their own gods too, and the explanation at the end of the verse reads like the chronicler's own comment. — Ellicott page

**v. 21**
- Ellicott: the numbers are large but believable for nomads, whose wealth was in herds. He compares King Mesha's tribute in 2 Kings 3:4 and says the figure for captives may be corrupted. — Ellicott page

**v. 22**
- Guzik: he links this to the unique wars of judgment God called Israel to bring against the Canaanites. He quotes Clarke that only a direct command from God could justify such a war, and that The Hagrites were full of idolatry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-4-8/
- JFB: the conquered lands were held from Saul until the Assyrian captivity, for about 300 years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-chronicles-5.html

**vv. 23–24**
- Matthew Henry: at first they held only Bashan, then they increased so much in wealth and power that they spread far north, even unto Hermon. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Ellicott: Baal-hermon may be Banias, and Senir is the Amorite name for Hermon. The bare list of names shows that much more historical material once existed. — Ellicott page

**v. 25**
- Matthew Henry: living on the border, they learned their idolatrous usages and transmitted the infection to the other tribes. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Ellicott: the Lord was Israel's husband, so the prophets call turning from him "whoredom." The chronicler sees the conquest of Canaan as God's work. — Ellicott page

**v. 26**
- Geneva Bible notes (Reformed): God stirred up the wicked and used them as instruments to execute his just judgment against sinners, although they were led by malice and ambition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-26.htm
- Benson (Methodist): God so governed his counsels and affections, that he brought his forces against this people rather than others. Poole says almost the same. Same URL. This is a small difference in emphasis between the Reformed and Methodist sources, not a real dispute.
- Matthew Henry: These tribes were first placed, and they were first displaced. They would have the best land, not considering that it lay most exposed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_005.cfm
- Ellicott: No trace of Pûl as distinct from Tiglath-pileser has been found in the Assyrian monuments. The chronicler probably means they are the same man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/5-26.htm
- JFB disagrees, calling Tiglath-pileser the son of the former. Keil says Pul attacked first but The deportation began, however, only with Tiglath-pileser. Same URL.
- BibleHub study notes: the exile fulfils the warning of Deuteronomy 28:36. "To this day" shows that, when Chronicles was written, the tribes had not returned to their ancestral lands. https://biblehub.com/study/1_chronicles/5-26.htm
